title: West Nile Virus Encephalitis in a Patient with Neuroendocrine Carcinoma
case_prompt:
A 58-year-old man presented in mid-summer after being found unconscious at home. He had one week of progressive gait instability but no other preceding neurologic or infectious symptoms.

His history was notable for poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma of the parotid gland diagnosed 7 months earlier, treated with seven cycles of chemotherapy (last dose 2 weeks earlier), and asymptomatic brain metastases identified 2 months before. He declined whole-brain radiation therapy. Other conditions included prostate cancer in remission, dyslipidemia, hypertension, and visual seizures on antiepileptic medication.

On examination he was somnolent but arousable, febrile (102.4°F), and tachycardic, with normal respiratory rate and oxygen saturation on 2 L/min nasal cannula. Neurologically, he was disoriented to time and place, dysarthric, amnestic, and had a new resting tremor in both upper extremities; there was no nuchal rigidity, focal weakness, or sensory deficits.

Laboratory tests showed mild hyponatremia and elevated creatine kinase, with normal liver function, blood count, and urinalysis. Urine drug screen was positive only for cannabinoids. Blood and urine cultures, chest radiography, and noncontrast head CT were unremarkable.

He was started on empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics and systemic glucocorticoids for possible infection or vasogenic edema, and his antiseizure medication was continued. After 24 hours his mental status partially improved, prompting suspicion of a seizure, but EEG revealed generalized background slowing without epileptogenic foci. Two days after presentation he remained febrile with persistent tremors but improved cognition. A lumbar puncture showed lymphocytic pleocytosis (95 cells/mm3, 8% neutrophils, 53% lymphocytes, 25% plasma cells, 14% monocytes), elevated glucose and protein; CSF Gram stain and cytology were negative, as were HSV-1/2 RT-PCR and Cryptococcus antigen. CSF and serum testing for West Nile virus IgM, IgG, and PCR were ordered.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Progression of brain metastases was initially considered — “Initially, there was suspicion for an infectious etiology or progression of previously known brain metastases; therefore, the patient was started on empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics and systemic glucocorticoids for potential vasogenic edema until further diagnostic evaluation could be performed.”  
2. Bacterial meningitis was considered but was unlikely given a lymphocytic CSF pleocytosis and negative Gram stain — “Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) studies revealed lymphocytic inflammation with an elevated glucose (84 mg/dL), elevated protein (89 mg/dL), and elevated total nucleated cell count (95/cumm), with a differential of neutrophils 8%, lymphocytes 53%, plasma cells 25%, and monocytes 14%. CSF Gram stain was negative…”  
3. A generalized seizure with postictal state was suspected but EEG did not show epileptiform activity — “The transient nature of his encephalopathy raised suspicion of a generalized seizure as the inciting event with resultant temporary postictal state. … EEG … revealing mild-to-moderate generalized background slowing, indicating diffuse encephalopathy, without any epileptogenic foci identified.”  
4. HSV encephalitis was excluded by negative PCR — “Herpes Simplex Virus-1 (HSV-1) and HSV-2 reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) tests were negative…”  
5. Cryptococcal meningoencephalitis was excluded by negative antigen testing — “as was Cryptococcus neoformans antigen.”  
6. West Nile virus neuroinvasive disease was diagnosed based on positive IgM despite negative PCR and IgG — “Although CSF IgG and PCR for WNV were negative, the patient's serum and CSF WNV IgM were qualitatively positive, establishing the diagnosis of WNV neuroinvasive disease.”
